hypotheses.observation: capacity_summary stores bound_type LOWER_BOUND, lower_inclusive 20, upper_exclusive null, capacity_knee null, and knee_reason KNEE_DETECTOR_NOT_IMPLEMENTED; the only stages present are r2-users5, r2-users10 and r2-users20, each with verdict PASS, achieved load equal to target (observed_min = observed_max = target on the p05_10s statistic, target_tolerance_ratio 0.1) and 30 of 30 expected bins complete.
hypotheses.possible_explanation: The load ladder stopped at 20 users and no knee detector ran, so this evidence cannot distinguish a system already near saturation just above 20 users from one with large headroom; both are consistent with the stored data.
hypotheses.recommended_check: Run additional stages above 20 users (e.g., 40, then 80) with the same windowing, bin-completeness and error-rate policy rules until a stage FAILs or latency degradation appears, and implement/enable the knee detector before quoting any capacity figure above 20 users.

hypotheses.observation: Per-window error policy checks record sample counts 30049 (r2-users5), 37550 (r2-users10) and 47404 (r2-users20), all with numerator 0; the window summaries bound windows of 300000 ms each (to_epoch_ms minus from_epoch_ms), giving derived throughputs of about 100, 125 and 158 samples per second, while active threads were flat at exactly 5, 10 and 20 (sample_standard_deviation 0).
hypotheses.possible_explanation: Per-user request rate may fall as concurrency rises - consistent with a latency- or pacing-bound closed workload (fixed think time) or with an unidentified bottleneck; because the stages run sequentially in time, warm-up or other time-based effects are confounded with load, so no single cause is established.
hypotheses.recommended_check: Compute per-stage latency percentiles and per-user request rates from per-window data and compare them against the JMeter pacing/think-time configuration; repeating the 5-user stage at the end of a run (or running a constant-load soak) would separate time from load effects.

hypotheses.observation: frontend cpu_cores interval means are 0.1818516 (r2-users5), 0.1893414666... (r2-users10) and 0.1881028 (r2-users20) cores, with per-window maxima 0.196647, 0.199595 and 0.198735 - essentially unchanged while the user count quadruples; by contrast checkoutservice means rise from 0.04700906... to 0.06844343... cores over the same stages.
hypotheses.possible_explanation: Frontend CPU may track requests per second rather than concurrent users (window throughput grew sublinearly), or a roughly constant background cost may dominate its usage, or the interval-mean aggregation may mask per-request changes; the stored summaries alone cannot distinguish these, and the sequential stages confound time with load.
hypotheses.recommended_check: Divide each window's frontend CPU mean by that window's derived sample throughput to compare per-request CPU cost across stages, and cross-check the request counts reaching the frontend against an independent metric source.

hypotheses.observation: paymentservice memory interval means rise across the sequential windows (32281941.3 to 33451281.07 to 33689645.5 bytes) with positive in-window slopes (13281.94, 978.04 and 78.64 bytes per second); frontend memory means rise 11957407.3 to 12937261.5 to 14036150.03 bytes, also with positive slopes; the run epoch delta is 1101178 ms.
hypotheses.possible_explanation: Gradual memory growth could be normal warm-up or allocation churn over the roughly 18-minute run, or a slow leak; because stages are sequential, growth may track elapsed time rather than user count, and no container limits appear in the evidence from which to judge proximity to saturation.
hypotheses.recommended_check: Run a constant-load soak at a single user count and track the memory slope over a longer horizon, or re-run a 5-user stage after the 20-user stage to see whether memory returns toward the earlier baseline; compare against actual container limits.
